chapter: Stagg's own story and the promotional society
title: Bunk Johnson Society, George Lewis visits and promoting tours, 1957-1967
summary: Stagg joins and takes over the Bunk Johnson Society, meets the George Lewis band, helps found the Promotional Society, becomes Barry Martin's manager and recalls tours by Harold Dejan, Sheik, Handy and the Eagle Brass Band session.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Graham Russell and a girl, Ray Whittrick, decided to form a Bunk Johnson Appreciation Society, and they were holding once a month meetings in a pub, the Porcupine, just off Charing Cross Road in London. I joined this with my brother at that time, who was beginning to play a little bit of banjo, and we joined it, and the first meeting we ever went to must have been in late 1958, when Graham Russell came out of the Air Force. The first records we heard were the folkways Music of New Orleans, and it was in 1958 I first heard the Bunk Jazz Informations, and managed to buy a copy of the Commodore as well at that time, of the Jazz Informations sites. This did a tremendous amount of good. This society had a membership of perhaps 200 or so. The London meetings only had about all 10 or 12 people turn up once a month, but we used to take records and exchange records and buy records, and this was a basis of all our collections, I think, at that time. Barry Martin turned up at these meetings at that time. He was a keen record collector then. I think we all acquired our first American Musics at that time, probably beaten up 78s at that time. The first LP I ever, American Music LP I bought was at that time, I paid a fantastic price for it, about £4. It was the Bunk 44 American Music, and I've still got the original one to this day, and I've only ever played it about once. I have two copies of it, and I've never played this original one more than about once or twice. It was a new one as well, and I was so proud of this. It was a new one as well, and I was so proud of this. These meetings, we had trouble at this pub we were using. We had to move to another pub, and gradually, less and less people came to these meetings petered out. But the Bunk Society still produced a newsletter and sold records, and we had our own record label at that time, known as Purist Records, which we had a sort of Bunk reissue programme. We had a couple of unused American Music sites issued on it, and some Bunk with Doc Evans we issued. We were very proud of these things, and mainly sold them only to members. There were about 5, 78s and 2 LPs issued over a period of about four years. This got me interested in record production and also a little bit of writing at that time. I used to write for one or two very short articles for a couple of magazines around at that time. One published in the Midlands in Birmingham by a guy called Les Page. And I did a little bit of writing for this small magazine. In about 1956 the Bunk-Johnson Society folded through lack of support. And things were pretty quiet from... around that time for a couple of years, and mainly stuck together. The people from the Society, we corresponded and exchanged records and news. George Lewis had turned up early in 1957, and we'd seen our first New Orleans musician. I can remember the Stoll Theatre in Kingsway in London, which has now been pulled down, all standing outside in the crowd, gazing in awe at George Lewis, who was the first New Orleans musician ever to come to this country. And he played some concerts with the King Collier Band. In late 1958, early 59, when the George Lewis Band turned up, George came with Kid Howard and Jim Robinson, Slowdrag, Joe Robichaud and Joe Watkins. We all turned out at Euston Station in London to see the band arrive. And this was our first real encounter with New Orleans musicians. We spoke to them and we had parties and we got to know them all personally. And this was a great thing. Before that time we only had such a few records in comparison with today, and there were only really names on record labels and on sleeves. We didn't know any of them personally. And we got to know them all personally. And we had some marvellous times. And I in particular travelled most of England following this band around. I saw about eight concerts out of the twelve. I think it was twelve they did, and I managed to get to about eight of them. Well that band went back, and they went out onto the continent and eventually went back. And I then, by this time I knew Barry Martin pretty well, because I'd met him through this Bunk Johnson Society, which had now folded. In early 1963 I decided to write to Ray Whittrick, who had been running this society, and asked what had happened about it. She still had the mailing list, one thing or another, but it was doing nothing. It was pretty stagnant. And she said, well if you want to take over the running of this society, by all means do so. I've still got all the mailing lists and all the people interested. The record side was defunct. So I took over the whole of the set-up of the Bunk Johnson Society, and for a couple of months produced a monthly newsletter. Decided it was pretty useless to carry on calling it the Bunk Johnson Society, because nothing was happening as far as Bunk Johnson was concerned. We were generally dealing with New Orleans music, so I changed it to the New Orleans Jazz Appreciation Society. And this society exists to this day, although it's pretty quiet and doesn't do a lot, but it keeps two, three hundred people informed of what's going on through letter, word of mouth, telephone calls, etc. etc. in England. In 1963, as was mentioned earlier, Kichik arrived, and it was decided that the only way to do this properly was to form another society. This is an idea of Barry Martins, to deal mainly with promoting New Orleans musicians in England, at that time only England. And the Promotional Society for New Orleans Music was formed. The first musicians to come over with this society was Kid Thomas and Emmanuel Paul. And they came to England in 1964. After this tour, a northern promoter became interested in this. He could see that there was something in England for this type of music, and decided that he would bring over George Lewis with this society of ours to tour with the Barry Martins band. And George Lewis came, I think, now, if I remember correctly, it was September 1964. And had an extensive tour and a recording session. And this 1964 tour was probably the foreignist tour that George Lewis made in England and the continent. Only in England was the Barry Martins band, but it was a very, very good tour. George was playing very well at that time in England. And this was probably the finest tour George made in England. In late 1964, Alton Purnell came, not promoted by the Promotional Society at all, but by Keith Smith. Keith Smith became interested in promoting, and entirely on his own, brought over Alton Purnell. In 1965, I officially became attached to the Promotional Society, and Don Smedley, sort of semi-officially became our official photographer, as he is now called. The first thing we all worked on together, that's the two of us and Barry Martins, was the Harold Dejan tour of 1965. And probably Harold had the most influence to the people in England. He was such a friendly guy, and mixed so well with the British public, and they accepted him so much. And although he turned up without a saxophone, and we had to hire him a horn, because we didn't dare bring him in. We were still avoiding board of trade and permits on one thing and another in those days. And he turned up just with his mouthpiece, which he told the customs people was his lucky charm. And we hired him a saxophone from some place in Wales. We had to go as far as Wales to find him a saxophone. And Don and I toured with Harold, well, all the jobs he played in England, which were down in Wales, a lot round the London area, and up to the north of England as well. He was so popular wherever he went. And Harold was the first musician in England to record with a brass band, and he called it the Young Olympia Brass Band, using only British musicians. The same day, he recorded a set of dance tunes, recorded live at a dance. This is the most peculiar dance, it was a works dance, and had people there ranging from 60 to about 16. And the impression we had was that this wouldn't go down at all well. None of the people there at all had heard of Harold Dejan or New Orleans music at all, but Harold turned up and completely took the place over in about five minutes flat. And it was quite an odd line-up as well, because Harold played alto, and we had Frank Brooker on tenor, John Coles on amplified guitar, Terry Knight on bass and Barry on drums, and it was a real little dance band sound. And from that day to this, that line-up hasn't been used in England at all. This is quite something. This was recorded at the time, live, and this was my first dabble in issuing records. I issued this particular recording with Barry Martin on a label which was known as New Orleans Anthology, which was a one and only effort because, again, we got into a bit of trouble with the performing rights society over it, and because we hadn't paid our dues on one thing and another. Although we paid for the session, we hadn't paid all the official things we had to be paid, so that was a one and only effort on that label. This was in 1965. In 19...we decided then that Harold being so popular and his first tour, discounting the George Lewis tour, which was promoted by an outside promoter, that these tours were going so well at that time, and the Barry Martin band in particular was very popular, that I joined...I became a partner in the promotional society, and I joined the Barry Martin organisation, became Barry's band manager, and also the one who looked after him on tour, looked after the band. We were on the road, did most of the driving on the road, and this was in late 65 and early 1966. The next tour we promoted in 1966 was again Kid Sheik, because he'd been pretty popular, and we brought over John Handy. This, again, was a very good tour. This was the first time that all his musicians had gone over to the continent, and Sheik and Handy went to Belgium, and this was the first time this had happened. They were very, very popular in Belgium, especially Handy. This was when Handy was becoming well-known outside his own country, and things were beginning to go well for him, you know, the other recordings, etc. This was a very good tour, it went well. It was followed, while Sheik and Handy were in England, Keith Smith, through a German promoter, Lippmann and Raal, decided to bring a band to Europe. And Alvin Elkhorn came with Jimmy Archie, Donnell Howard, Elton Pennell again, Saif Frazier and Pops Foster. This was the last tour that Donnell Howard was to make, of course. He died shortly after, and not long after, Jimmy Archie. While they were here working for Keith Smith in England, Keith Smith covered the English side of this tour for the German promoters. Sheik and Handy still being here, we had quite an epic recording session, known as the Eagle Brass Band. We recorded inside, using Sheik and Alvin Elkhorn, and Keith Smith on trumpets, Saif Frazier on bass drum, and Barry Martin on snares, Handy on alto, and the rest was made up of local musicians. Jim Young on tuba, who later recorded with the Olympia Brass Band. This was recorded for George Buck, who to this day hasn't issued this session yet, but it's a very, very fine session, and quite a historic session, as far as English recordings go. And this brings us up to 1967, when we worked on a tour and brought Lewis Nelson to England. Now, Nelson had a very good tour of England, and also went to Belgium. We tied up with some Italian people, who were not promoters, but just enthusiasts. They'd heard a couple of New Orleans records, and when I say a couple, this is literally true.
